You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

We report a method for the precise regulation of intracrystalline missing-linkers to control the
permeability and selectivity of metal-organic framework (MOF) membranes. The method is
applied for the design of stable ceramic-based MOF-801 membranes for hypersaline water
treatment via pervaporation. For efficient membrane growth, an in situ nano-seeding strategy was
employed to provide nucleation sites followed by surfactant posttreatment to minimize cracks.
Missing-linkers are regulated in MOF-801 membranes by altering the ratio of fumarate to formic
acid, which positively enhances water transport by modifying the MOF-801 structure and
chemistry. Specifically, missing-linkers enhance membrane structural hydrophilicity with stronger
host-guest interaction energy, resulting in faster transport with a lower energy barrier by enlarging
the pore window and pore cage. The MOF-801 membranes demonstrated near-perfect salt
rejection (~99.9%) and high water flux, outperform most state-of-the-art silica, MOF, and
zeolite polycrystalline membranes for the treatment of both saline and hypersaline waters. Notably,
the membranes exhibited stable desalination performance, highlighting their promising application
potential. This work provides a strategy for the rational design of next-generation high-
performance MOF nanochannel membranes for challenging water purification applications.

---

## Introduction

To combat global water scarcity, desalination will play a critical role in tapping into
unconventional water sources.1,2 While reverse osmosis (RO) is the current paradigm for
desalination, conventional RO cannot be used for hypersaline waters (salinity > ~10 wt.%) due to
the ultrahigh osmotic pressures that must be overcome, which exceed the maximum hydraulic
pressures that can be applied.3-6 At these higher salinities, thermally-driven membrane processes
have an advantage over RO as their operation is less sensitive to salinity.7-9 A promising chemical-
potential-driven membrane process is pervaporation (PV).10 A liquid feed stream (heated in some
cases) is exposed to one side of the PV membrane and a vacuum is applied to the other. Under
these conditions, water traverses the PV membrane, vaporizes, and then condensed at the permeate
side.9,11,12 In this process, dissolved salts are retained because salts, unlike water, have negligible
vapor pressure at the operational temperatures and pressures of pervaporation. PV is capable of
treating hypersaline waters, even when operated at ambient temperatures.13,14 Unlike conventional
membrane distillation (MD) processes, a more robust PV process has advantages in addressing
challenges like wetting, scaling, and fouling, which enables promising operational performance.15

A major challenge for PV desalination is the design of high-performance separation
membranes featuring high permeability, salt rejection, and operating stability.9,16,17 Unlike their
polymer counterparts, more robust inorganic polycrystalline nanoporous membranes, such as
zeolite and silica, have been proposed.18,19 While these membranes offered stable desalination
performance, they suffered from low permeability, even for the treatment of seawater or low-
salinity wastewaters. In contrast, metal-organic framework (MOF) membranes have well-defined
nanochannel structures, abundant affinity sites, modular nature for functionalities, and structural
stability, thereby enabling high uptake of water and promising separation performance.20-23
Compared with state-of-the-art water-stable MOFs, MOF-801 demonstrates highly robust
characteristics, rapid water adsorption rate, and high water harvesting capacity.24-28 In addition,
MOF-801 inherently possesses a suitable crystallographic structure where the pore window size
(3.5 Å) ranges between water molecules (2.8 Å) and hydrated sodium ions (~ 7.16 Å). This makes
MOF-801 a promising candidate for desalination membranes with precise separation ability, which
has not been experimentally demonstrated until now. However, the fabrication of a well-
intergrown (i.e., crack-free or intercrystalline-defect-free) pure MOF-801 membrane is
experimentally difficult and thus lags behind its mixed-matrix membrane and other MOF
membrane counterparts.

Rational tailoring of crystalline chemistry of MOF membranes has the potential to
substantially improve membrane functionality and performance, but is considered to be
particularly challenging. Recently, intracrystalline defects, such as missing linkers and missing
clusters, have been synthesized and confirmed to influence the permeability or selectivity of MOF
liquid- or gas-separation membranes.29-33 However, the precise creation of favorable
intracrystalline defects is challenging and has not been well-studied in membrane-based separation
applications. Moreover, it remains unclear how intracrystalline missing linkers affect separation
performance, such as selectivity and permeability, at the molecular or atomic level. Therefore,
elucidating these transport mechanisms is critical for the rational design of nanoscale channels
with tailorable structure and chemistry in next-generation MOF membranes. Unlike the
elimination of intracrystalline lattice defects to improve the selectivity of MOF membranes 27, the
aim of this work is to precisely regulate intracrystalline missing linkers of MOF membranes to
enhance the permeation of water molecules while maintaining high salt rejection. Differing from
a former study that introduced an arbitrary number of missing linkers (~23.5%),30 this work
demonstrates that precise regulation of missing linkers to enhance water transport could be realized
in MOF-801 membranes, which is not only practically challenging, but also critical for
understanding fundamental mass transport phenomena.

In this work, we report a robust protocol for well-intergrown MOF-801 nanochannel thin
membranes with precise regulation of intracrystalline missing linkers for enhanced water
permeability via pervaporation. We further provide a mechanistic understanding of the missing-
linker enhancement of water permeation, where missing linkers not only enhance structural
hydrophilicity (i.e., water adsorption ability) but also render faster water transport via altering the
pore structure and chemistry of the nanoscale MOF-801 channels. The membranes exhibit
complete salt rejection, operation stability, and higher water flux in comparison to state-of-the-art
silica, MOF, and zeolite membranes for the treatment of saline and hypersaline waters. Notably,
the MOF-801 membranes demonstrated resilient performance under challenging water treatment
conditions, including high temperatures, highly oxidizing environments, and in the presence of
oils and surfactants.

---

## Results

Design and Characterization of Crack-free MOF-801 Membrane
Engineering the structure and surface properties of substrates is crucial for subsequent MOF
membrane growth and application. In this work, crack-free MOF-801 membranes were fabricated
by a secondary growth method followed by surfactant Span80 posttreatment for PV desalination
(Figure 1, Supplementary Figures 1-3). Ceramic substrates (α-Al2O3:average pore size ~700 nm;
ZrO2: average pore size ~ 142 nm) were specially designed with a hollow fiber configuration for
PV, featuring an ultrahigh packing density (~4000 m2·m-3) that is 16-40 times higher than those of
tubular (200-250 m2·m-3) or flat-sheet (100-150 m2·m-3) commercial substrates; with the latter
most commonly used as the substrate for current MOF membranes (Figure 1a, Supplementary
Figure 4, SI Section 1.2).34 To modify the substrate and enable the growth of well-intergrown
MOF-801 membranes, a more hydrophilic nano-TiO2 interlayer was introduced with lowered
surface roughness (Ra ~68 nm) (Supplementary Figure 4) and average pore size (~105 nm). Such
a TiO2 interlayer could provide a modified substrate surface with more hydroxyl groups and thus
more nucleation sites for MOF crystal nucleation and subsequent growth, which is beneficial to
the formation of thin, well-intergrown MOF-801 membranes. MOF-801 was selected to be
fabricated into a separation membrane because of its stability toward some solvents, especially
hypersaline solutions at elevated temperatures (Supplementary Figure 5). Although there were
only minor and negligible additional peaks for the samples after exposure in DMF, acetone, and
water—the phase structure degraded to some extent in strongly acidic aqueous solution (pH 0.7),
which can be reflected by peak broadening and new peaks arising (Supplementary Figure 5).
Nevertheless, such chemically harsh condition is far beyond practical application conditions. In
this work, a nanoseed-induced secondary growth method (seed size: ~69 nm, Supplementary
Figure 6) was employed to fabricate the polycrystalline MOF-801 membrane to increase the
presence of active nucleation sites and reduce the energy barrier for nucleation based on Ostwald’s
rule.35

One key challenge is the generation of macroscopic cracks inside MOF-801 membranes during
drying after membrane growth (Figures 1a, 1b), which inevitably undermines the separation
performance. To address this issue, a surfactant (Span80) posttreatment was employed to
effectively avoid the formation of cracks (Figures 1a, 1c, Supplementary Figure 7). For the
polycrystalline MOF-801 membrane, cracks formed due to the increased capillary stress between
intergrown MOF crystals during the solvent evaporation stage.36 However, after being soaked in a
Span80 chloroform solution for 2 days, high-quality MOF-801 membranes (thickness ~1.67 μm)
with a pure MOF-801 phase were obtained on a TiO2 interlayer-modified ceramic substrate with
visible and distinct boundaries (Figures 1d, 1g), which were free of macroscopic intracrystalline
cracks (Figure 1c). Posttreatment of the MOF-801 membrane with Span80 significantly
suppressed the evaporation rate of residual solvents (N,N-dimethyl formamide, formic acid) and
reduced capillary stress, consequently minimizing the formation of cracks. Unlike the unmodified
MOF-801 membrane (“cracked”), which exhibits poor gas selectivity, the modified MOF-801
membrane is well-intergrown (i.e., without macroscopic cracks or other intercrystalline defects)
since its ideal gas selectivities (H2/N2: 7.6, H2/CH4: 16.5, N2/CH4: 2.2) are all higher than the
Knudsen diffusion selectivities (H2/N2: 3.7, H2/CH4: 2.8, N2/CH4: 1.3) (Figure 1e).

The ATR-FTIR spectrum of the modified MOF-801 membrane verifies the presence of the -
C=O-O bond (1400 cm-1, 1577 cm-1) and -C=O-OH group (1213 cm-1) of the MOF-801
structure,37,38 as well as the in-plane deformation vibration of C-H (2852-2856 cm-1, 2921−2925
cm-1) and strong stretching vibration of ester bonds (1734−1742 cm -1) of the Span80 structure
(Figure 1f).39 Nevertheless, Span80 posttreatment did not significantly change the pore size (6 Å
vs. 6 Å) and specific surface area (499 m2·g-1 vs. 535.5 m2·g-1) of MOF-801 (Supplementary Figure
8), which indicates that such a surfactant posttreatment modification would not negatively affect
the pore structure of the membranes. Additionally, the presence of O, Ti, Zr, and C signals in the
XPS spectra are clearly identified for the TiO2 interlayer, cracked MOF-801, and crack-free MOF-
801 membranes (Supplementary Figure 9). Ti was detected in the TiO2
nano-interlayer surface,
while Zr was detected in the membrane surface of both cracked and crack-free MOF-801
membranes (Supplementary Figures 9, 10). Moreover, even after strong ultrasonication treatment
(150 W, 20 min) for an accelerated stability test, the MOF-801-1.43 membrane maintained
integrated surface and cross-sectional structural morphologies, indicating promising mechanical
stability for practical operation Supplementary Figure 11).

Precise Regulation of Intracrystalline Missing Linkers
Although missing linkers have been experimentally designed in UiO-66 MOF membranes,
precise regulation of intracrystalline missing linkers has not been reported until now.32 Without the
addition of a modulator, it is difficult to form highly crystalline MOF-801 membrane (usually only
some amorphous phase) from ZrOCl2 and fumarate due to the slow crystallization kinetics.40 The
amorphous phase on substrates is not suitable for pervaporation desalination since it does not form
a membrane layer with defined MOF crystalline structure comprised of regular pore window and
pore cage to allow for water molecule transport and salt rejection. By contrast, our current work,
employs formic acid as a modulator to not only accelerate the crystallization of MOF-801, but also
precisely regulate intracrystalline missing linkers by adjusting the ratio of fumarate to formic acid
(Figure 2, Supplementary Figure 12). The intracrystalline missing linkers were first identified and
quantified based on the results of X-Ray diffraction (XRD), 1H Nuclear Magnetic Resonance
(NMR), 13C Magic Angle Spinning (MAS) NMR, and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) (Figures
2b-2e, Supplementary Figures 13-15). By adjusting the ratios of fumarate to formic acid (10:400,
6:400, 4:400, 2:400 and 1:400), the frequency of missing linkers per Zr6 crystalline formula unit
(denoted as linker deficiency unless specified) can be precisely regulated and was determined to
be 0.32, 0.70, 1.25, 1.43, and 1.62, based on the TGA results (denoted as MOF-801-0.32, MOF-
801-0.70, MOF-801-1.25, MOF-801-1.43, and MOF-801-1.62 in this work) (Figure 2b).

The TGA results indicated that a deficiency was present in all samples due to deviations in
mass loss behavior in comparison to the ideal plateau of MOF-801 (Supplementary Figure 13).41
The presence of missing clusters were ruled out according to the XRD patterns where no reo phase
was observed between 2 and 8° (2θ) (Figure 2c).42 Therefore, we can conclude that the
intracrystalline defects are the result of missing linkers. In addition to fumarate molecules, the
presence of HCOO- (formic molecule) can be experimentally confirmed by the 1H NMR spectra
(Figure 2d), indicating the occurrence of a competitive coordination reaction between the Zr6
cluster and formic acid. This can be ascribed to the fact that during the solvothermal reaction,
formic acid coordinates with Zr6 clusters via carboxyl groups by competing with fumarate acid to
form the missing fumarate linkers.

With increasing missing-linker density, the pore structure of MOF-801 was enlarged, which
was confirmed by the near-linear increase in pore size (i.e., pore width, from 4.62 to 5.09 Å), total
pore volume (from 0.36 to 0.68 cm-3∙g-1), and specific surface area (from 292.1 to 791.1 m-2∙g-1)
(Figures 2e, 2f, Supplementary Figure 14). Moreover, the water uptake capacity was enhanced
with the increasing presence of missing linkers (Figure 2f), which is not only a result of the
enlarged pore structure but also the generation of more hydrophilic sites with enhanced water
adsorption ability. For the pervaporation desalination process (Supplementary Figure 3), the
presence of missing linkers reduced the activation energy barrier required for water molecule
transport across the membranes (Supplementary Figure 16). Furthermore, the water flux of MOF-
801 membranes linearly increased with increasing linker deficiency under constant operational
temperatures (40-80℃), while salt rejection remains nearly complete, in the range of 99.69% -
99.91% under all operational temperatures (Figure 2g). Specifically, when the linker deficiency
increases from 0.32 to 1.43, the water flux is enhanced by ~60% at 80℃. Additionally, increasing
the operational temperature from 40 to 80℃ improves the water flux from 12.3 to 35.6 L∙m-2∙h-1
at a 1.43 linker deficiency due to the enhanced driving force. The performance of the membrane
with the highest linker deficiency 1.62 is not shown since it was synthesized under strongly acidic
conditions, resulting in poor membrane quality and desalination performance.

Atomistic Mechanism for Missing-Linker Enhanced Performance
To shed light on the effect of missing linkers on desalination performance, state-of-the-art
molecular simulations, including molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo, associated with
experimental data were employed to offer atomistic insights into the permeation mechanism of
water molecules through MOF-801 membranes (Figure 3, SI Section 3.1). To reveal the role of
missing linkers, we investigated a defect-free simulation structure and two highly symmetric
missing-linker simulation structures with theoretical deficiency of 1/12 and 1/4 (also denoted
MOF-801-DF, MOF-801-0.5, and MOF-801-1.5, respectively). Through these simulations, the
improvement in water flux was ascribed to missing linkers not only enhancing water adsorption
(i.e., water affinity) but also water transport by altering the intracrystalline pore microenvironment
(i.e., more hydrophilic active sites) and structure (i.e., both enlarged pore window and pore cage)
of the subnanometer channels in the MOF-801 framework structure. Reducing the activation
energy barrier, the presence of missing linkers enables the ultrafast transport of more water
molecules (Figures 3a−3e). Missing linkers also enhance the structural hydrophilicity of the MOF
frameworks due to the exposure of more water adsorption sites (i.e., [Zr6(OH)4O4] cluster),
resulting in a higher water uptake rate and higher water loading (Figures 3f, 3g, SI Section 3.2).

To gain insight into such an enhancement from an energetic point of view, Monte Carlo
simulations were conducted to sample the interaction energy between a single water molecule and
MOF-801 framework structures. The interaction energy distribution for MOF-801-0.5 and MOF-
801-1.5 indicated stronger interactions resulting from water-framework Coulombic interactions
when compared to MOF-801-DF (Figure 3h). As a result, MOF-801 exhibited 4-16 times higher
adsorption capacity when compared with other state-of-the-art, water-stable MOFs (i.e., ML-UiO-
66, UiO-66, UiO-66-NH2) (Figure 3i). During the PV process, the creation of more missing linkers
enhances the permeation dynamics of more water molecules inside the membranes (Figure 3j).
Theoretically, the water flux significantly increases from 16.4 to 36.4 L·m−1·h−1 with increasing
missing linker deficiency from 0 to 1.5 (Figure 3k). We can, therefore, conclude that
intracrystalline missing linkers in the MOF-801 membrane not only promote the structural
hydrophilicity (i.e., water adsorption ability) but also render faster transport dynamics (i.e.,
diffusion ability) of water molecules. These two aspects result in the higher water flux of MOF-
801 membranes with more missing linkers than was observed experimentally. As previously noted,
the MOF-801-1.62 membrane synthesized under strongly acidic conditions exhibit poor
desalination performance. Thus, the high-quality MOF-801-1.43 membrane was selected for
subsequent performance and stability evaluation and will be referred to as MOF-801 membrane
unless specified hereafter.

Promising Desalination Performance and Operation Stability
The MOF-801 membranes exhibited exceptional desalination performance and operation
stability for the treatment of saline waters in a wide range of concentrations (0-10 wt.% NaCl)
(Figure 4). Independent of salt concentration and operation temperature, the rejection of all MOF-
801 membranes are over 99.9%, resulting in permeate salt concentrations of 2-44 ppm, which are
lower than the product water quality standards of both China and the WHO for desalination
techniques (China HY/T 247-2018: 50 ppm (salt concentration), WHO: 1,200 ppm (total dissolved
solids)) (Supplementary Figure 17).9 This performance indicates that the MOF-801 membranes
could effectively desalinate brines to produce clean water by PV (Figures 4a, S3). The pore size of
MOF-801-1.43 was determined to be 5.07 Å (Figure 2d, Supplementary Figure 14b), which is
lower than the size of hydrated ions (d [Na+·(H2O)n] ~ 0.716 nm, d [Cl-·(H2O)n] ~ 0.664 nm).43
The near-complete salt rejections could be ascribed to the fact that the salt ions have negligible
vapor pressure at the operating conditions, and did not vaporize in the pervaporation process.

In particular, even at approximately room temperature (30°C) (without heat energy input on the
feed side), water flux is still very promising (e.g., 6.3 Lm-2·h-1 for 3.5 wt.% saline water, 3.9 Lm-
2·h-1 for 10 wt.% hypersaline water) (Figure 4a). This energy-saving feature is different from the
MD process, where the water flux (~1 Lm-2·h-1) is often negligible at room temperature.54 For
saline waters with the same concentration, water flux was further enhanced with operation
temperature (from 30 to 70°C) due to an enhanced driving force of the adsorption-diffusion process
of water molecules, since PV is a typical thermal activation adsorption-diffusion process.49 The
activation energy (Eact.) is approximately 3.69 kJ·mol−1 for 3.5 wt.% saline water (Supplementary
Figure 17), which is less than those of other PV processes.49 At the same operating temperature,
the water flux was demonstrated to show a declining trend with increasing feed salt concentration
(Figure 4a).50 This phenomenon is attributed to the elevated salt concentration at the vaporization
interface, where fewer free water molecules are transported across the MOF-801 membrane
because more water molecules are bound to salt ions to form a hydration shell. Moreover, the
MOF-801-1.43 membrane showed high water flux (27.4 Lm-2·h-1) for treating saline waters (3.5
wt.% NaCl), outperforming most state-of-the-art silica, zeolite, and MOF membranes (1-10 Lm-
2·h-1) (Figure 4b). Unlike other studies focusing on 3.5 wt.% NaCl saline water treatment, the
MOF-801 membrane exhibited promising water flux (10.5 Lm-2·h-1) for even more challenging
hypersaline waters (10 wt.%), which are 1.6–7.4 times that of current zeolite and MOF membranes
(Figure 4c). Like the water flux, the water permeance of the MOF-801 membranes were enhanced
with linker deficiencies but decreased with salt concentration (Supplementary Figure 18).

Differentiating from most other MOF membranes that suffer from insufficient water stability,
MOF-801 membranes demonstrate stable operational performance (in both flux and rejection) and
acceptable structural integrity (in both MOF-801 crystalline phase and membrane morphology)
for the treatment of 7 wt.% hypersaline water at 70°C for 120 h (Figures 4d, 4f, 4 g).55 Under XRD,
the MOF-801 membranes exhibited two characteristic reflections of MOF-801 phase between 7
and 11° before and after operation, indicating some stability in their phase crystalline structure
(Figure 4f). However, some peak width broadening was found from 0.24 to 0.37 especially after
108 h exposure at pH 3, which reflected a change in the lattice structure to some extent (i.e., crystal
lattice grain sizes might decrease slightly), while the peaks were nearly unchanged in the case of
hypersaline water exposure. The efficient treatment of harsh environmental wastewaters can be
challenging for conventional membranes. However, after soaking in an acidic hypersaline solution
(pH=3, 10 wt % NaCl), the MOF-801 membrane still exhibited stable flux and salt rejection over
~100 h of operation (Figure 4e). Even after constant operation in harsh environments (e.g., high
temperature, high salinity, and low pH ∼3), the MOF-801 membrane showed good structural
integrity, which was confirmed by its resilient surface morphology, phase composition, and high
ideal gas selectivity (Figures 4f, 4g, Supplementary Figure 19). These results indicate that MOF-
801 membranes are promising candidates for the production of clean water from hypersaline brines
via PV.

To further investigate the resilience of the MOF-801 membrane, desalination performance and
operation stability were evaluated under harsh treatment conditions using acidic brines, industrial
wastewaters, and oxidizing brines (Figure 5). Acidic hypersaline waters with an initial pH of 3
could be concentrated to the point of crystallization by using MOF-801 membranes at an operating
temperature of 70℃, all while consistently producing pure water on the permeate side of the
membrane (Figure 5a, Supplementary Figure 20). During operation, the water flux gradually
decreased from 10.5 to 2.6 Lm-2·h-1 due to the decreasing driving force caused by the feed being
concentrated 4.45-fold, all while salt rejection was maintained above 99.9%.

The treatment of real industrial acidic saline wastewater (pH ~3.4) can also be challenging for
conventional membranes because of its complicated composition (Supplementary Table 5).
Interestingly, the MOF-801 membrane exhibits promisingly stable performance under these
conditions (Figure 5b). The water flux first decreased from its initial value of ~ 10.4 L m–2 h–1 and
then remained relatively stable in the range of ~ 5.0 – 6.0 L m–2 h–1due to the membrane fouling
at the vaporization interface (i.e., membrane surface). By using a simple DI water cleaning method,
the water flux of the MOF-801 membranes could be efficiently recovered to 9.85 L m–2 h–1 (with
a recovery ratio of ~ 94%). In addition to having a stable water flux, the membrane shows high
rejection of all salt ions, such as Na+, K+, Mg2+, and Ca2+ (all above 99.0%), which can be ascribed
to that fact that salt ions have negligible vapor pressure, and did not vaporize during the
pervaporation process.

One of the major challenges for conventional polyamide membranes is their susceptibility to
chlorine oxidation.56 Unlike polyamide membranes, the MOF-801 membranes showed a highly
stable desalination performance for hypersaline water feed even at 70℃ after exposure to 100 ppm
NaClO aqueous solution for as long as 21 days (i.e., equivalent to 50,400 ppm·h chlorine exposure)
(Figure 5c); indicating a significantly improved chlorine resistance (1.7 – 20.0 times higher) than
both commercial and state-of-the-art polyamide membranes (2,500 – 30,430 ppm·h chlorine
exposure).57,58 After continuous operation under these different extreme conditions, all the MOF-
801 membranes retained their integrity as exhibited by the ideal selectivities of H2/N2 gases, which
were still higher than their Knudsen diffusion selectivity (H2/N2: 3.7) (Figure 5f, Supplementary
Figure 21). Moreover, the MOF-801 membranes exhibited stability in both the crystalline phase
and membrane structure, which is reflected by the XRD (only except for slight peak-width
broadening), 1H NMR spectra, ATR-FTIR spectra, and membrane surface morphology (Figures
5d, 5e, 5g, 5h). The performance stability can be ascribed to the highly stable membrane structure
consisting of well intergrown MOF-801 crystals in which there are highly robust Zr–O covalent
bonds, and strong coordination bonds between [Zr6(OH)4O4] cluster (i.e., Lewis acid) and
fumarate linker (i.e., Lewis base). Additionally, unlike commercial polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)
distillation membranes (Nanjing CAS-Bidun Newmen Technology Co., Ltd., China), the MOF-
801 pervaporation membranes show better desalination performance and operating stability for
treating more challenging hypersaline waters containing low surface tension species, including oil
and surfactant (Supplementary Figure 22). This is similar to what was previously reported between
commercial PTFE distillation membranes and polymeric pervaporation membranes.59 This
resilient desalination performance under various harsh conditions indicates the application
potential of the robust MOF-801 membranes in a wide range of industrial applications.

---

## Methods

In situ Synthesis of MOF-801 Nanoseed Layer
Both Al2O3 and ZrO2 ceramic substrates (100-200 pieces for each membrane) were first fabricated
by an immersion-induced phase inversion process, followed by complete drying and sintering at
1550°C for 4 h (Al2O3) or at 1050°C for 2 h (ZrO2). A TiO2 interlayer was then coated onto the
substrates by a dip-coating method, followed by complete drying and sintering at 800°C for 4 h.
Then, a thin layer of uniformly dispersed MOF-801 nanoseeds (size ~69 nm) was synthesized in
situ on the outer surface of TiO2 interlayer-modified ceramic substrates via the solvothermal
method. Specifically, fumaric acid and ZrOCl2·8H2O were first dissolved into a solvent mixture
of DMF and formic acid. Then, the substrates with both sides sealed were placed into the mixture
solution inside a 100 mL Teflon reactor for the solvothermal reaction at 120°C for 24 h to form a
MOF-801 nanoseed layer in situ. Finally, after the reaction was allowed to cool, the samples were
cleaned with DMF.

Preparation of Crack-free MOF-801 Membrane
MOF-801 membranes with different missing linkers (10-20 pieces for each membrane
composition) were synthesized via a solvothermal secondary growth method, followed by
surfactant posttreatment. To create different missing-linker densities, fumaric acid (0.1420 g,
0.4260 g, 0.7087 g) and formic acid (9 mL) at different molar ratios (fumaric acid: formic acid =
2:400, 6:400, 10:400) were first mixed with DMF (61 mL) and ZrOCl2·8H2O (0.4025 g). Then,
the substrates coated with a MOF-801 nanoseed layer were placed into the mixture solution inside
a 100 mL Teflon reactor for solvothermal reaction at 120°C for 24 h to allow for the secondary
growth of MOF-801 membranes. Finally, after the reaction, the MOF-801 membranes were
cleaned with DMF and dried at room temperature for 6 h to produce the cracked MOF-801
membranes. To avoid the formation of cracks, the synthesized MOF-801 membranes were
immediately immersed into a Span80 solution (1 g Span80 dissolved in 10 mL chloroform) for 24
h prior to drying. The MOF-801 membranes were completely dried in a chloroform atmosphere
for 72 h and then activated to remove any solvent molecules (DMF) at 150°C for 24 h under
vacuum (-1 bar).

Membrane Performance Evaluation
The desalination performance of MOF-801 membranes (effective membrane area ~100-200 mm2)
was evaluated in a lab-scale pervaporation (PV) setup with various saline waters (1.5, 3.5, 7 wt. %
NaCl, pH 7), hypersaline water (10 wt.% NaCl, pH 7), acidic hypersaline water (10 wt.% NaCl,
pH 3), and real industrial acidic saline wastewater (A machinery factory, Dalian City, Liaoning
Province, China) as the feeds (feed water reservoir volume ~100-250 ml) (Supplementary Figure
3). The pervaporation system was first stabilized for ~2 h. The feed flow rate was controlled at 160
±5 mL min–1 by a peristaltic pump, while a vacuum of (~60 Pa) was applied on the permeate side.
A cold trap was utilized to cool and collect the permeate water after condensation at different time
intervals (~2h). The permeate flux (Jw, L·m-2·h-1) was determined at a certain time interval (Δt, h)
based on the volume of the condensed permeate (ΔV, L) across a constant effective membrane area
(A, m2) according to Eq. (1). During membrane operation, the salt concentration of the solution
was measured using a conductivity meter (DDSJ-308A, Shanghai REX Instrument Factory, China).
The conductivity of the feed solution was used to calculate the salt concentration based on a
calibration curve. Salt rejection was determined according to Eq. 2, where Cf (mg·L−1) and Cp
(mg·L−1) are the salt concentrations of the permeate and feed, respectively:

Jw = ΔV / (A * Δt) (1)
R = (Cf - Cp) / Cf (2)

Molecular Simulations
Classical molecular dynamics simulations, implemented in the LAMMPS package, were
conducted to investigate the pervaporation desalination mechanism of MOF-801-DF, MOF-801-
0.5, and MOF-801-1.5 membranes.60 The simulation system and results are described in detail in
SI Section 3 (Supplementary Figures 23,24).

Pervaporation simulations were carried out in a canonical ensemble (i.e., NVT) at a temperature
of 343 K with a time step of 1 fs. The system’s temperature was modulated using the Nosé‒Hoover
thermostat with a damping factor of 100 time steps (i.e., 100 fs). For each simulation, energy
minimization was first carried out to preliminarily relax the system. Subsequently, a hydrostatic
pressure of 1 atm was applied on the feed pistons, and a molecular dynamics simulation was
performed for 40 ns to bring the liquid density closer to its equilibrium value (i.e., 1.0 g cm−3) and
to fully saturate the initially empty membrane structure with saline solution. Finally, the systems
were further equilibrated for 5 ps, followed by a production run of 20 ps at a constant pressure of
1 atm. We should note that all of the studied membranes, as well as the piston and adsorbing plate,
were assumed to be rigid.

Characterization
The structural morphology or element composition of MOF-801 membranes and ceramic
substrates were characterized in a field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM) (S-4800,
Hitachi, Japan; NOVA NanoSEM 450, FEI Company, USA) equipped with an energy dispersive
spectrometer (EDS). X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements were carried out in an Ultima IV X-
ray diffractometer using Cu-Kα radiation with a step size of 0.02° and 2 s per step (D/Max-2400,
Rigaku, Japan). The functional groups of the MOF-801 membrane and powder were analyzed by
attenuated total reflectance-Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR) (IS50, Thermo
Nicolet, US). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was used for analysis of elements using a
Thermo Fisher K-Alpha spectrometer (K-Alpha, Thermo Fisher, USA). Thermogravimetric
analysis (TGA) was carried out in a thermal analyzer (TG/DTA 6300, Seiko Co., Ltd., Japan) at a
heating rate of 5°C min-1 from room temperature (~25℃) to 700°C in air. Liquid 1H nuclear
magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra were recorded in a nuclear magnetic resonance spectrometer
(Bruker Advance Ⅲ500, Bruker, Switzerland). The nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherms of
MOF-801 crystals were recorded in an automatic physical adsorption apparatus (AS-1-MP-11,
Quantachrome, USA). Dynamic vapor sorption (DVS, Surface Measurement System Ltd., UK)
was used to measure the water uptake behaviors of MOF-801 and Span80-posttreated MOF-801
crystals, as well as UiO-66 and UiO-66-NH2.

Other detailed characterization can be found in the Supplementary Materials (SI Section 1.4).

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript reports a novel approach to enhancing the permeability and selectivity of MOF-801 membranes through the precise regulation of intracrystalline missing-linker defects, which is a significant contribution to the field of water desalination technology. The method of employing an in situ nano-seeding strategy alongside surfactant post-treatment to minimize crack formation represents a notable advance in MOF membrane fabrication. The research's innovation is further underscored by its application to hypersaline water treatment via pervaporation, demonstrating exceptional performance metrics, including near-perfect salt rejection (~99.8%) and high water flux (12.3 L∙m^-2∙h^-1 at 40℃), setting a new standard in the field.
The authors should consider the following concerns:
1. DThe manuscript briefly mentions the impact of defect regulation on membrane performance but lacks a detailed explanation or theoretical model. What specific interactions at the molecular level lead to enhanced water transport and selectivity? A more rigorous theoretical framework or simulation data supporting these claims is suggested.
2. Control group comparisons: While the performance improvements are highlighted, the manuscript does not provide a detailed comparison with control groups lacking the precise regulation of missing-linker defects. How does the performance of unmodified MOF-801 membranes compare, and what is the quantitative impact of your innovations?
3. The detailed performance data regarding flux and reject should be presented in Abstract.
4. The authors briefly claim that this membrane outperforms state-of-the-art silica, MOF, and zeolite polycrystalline membranes for the treatment of both saline and hypersaline waters. Is it true? More supporting data or broader literature review should be presented.
5. The economic analysis provided is overly simplistic and does not account for scale-up challenges, raw material costs, or operational expenses over the membrane's lifecycle. Can the authors expand this analysis to include a detailed cost breakdown and a comparison with existing desalination technologies??
6. The performance stability under different environmental conditions (e.g., extreme pH, high temperatures, biofouling potential) is not adequately addressed. How does the membrane's performance vary under these stress conditions, and what mechanisms ensure its stability? Please briefly discuss this issue.
Given the manuscript's substantial contributions and innovative approaches to MOF membrane technology for water purification, I recommend a moderate revision.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript should be immediately rejected by Nature Communications, with no opportunity for reconsideration. This manuscript is most well suited for publication in a specialized disciplinary journal, such as the Journal of Membrane Science or Desalination or other membrane or water purification focused journal.
There is an overall lack of novelty in this paper and the results of this work are not of enough significance to be reported in Nature Communications, despite this possibly being the first report of using the material MOF-801 for pervaporation desalination.
Many molecular sieves and polymers have previously been reported for pervaporation desalination, and have performance superior to that of the membranes reported by this manuscript. In addition to having superior performance, the previously reported membranes (often polymers or nanocomposites) have much simpler manufacturing capability and potential for successful commercial scale up.
The authors of this paper seem to be unaware of the extensive body of literature on the topic of pervaporation desalination and are referred to Table 2 of the excellent review paper “Desalination by membrane pervaporation: A Review” Desalination, 547, 1, 116223, doi:10.1016/j.desal.2022.116223 (which is not cited by this manuscript). Table 2 of the referenced review paper provides a comprehensive summary of performance of >50 distinct pervaporation desalination membranes. As can be seen from this summary table multiple of the previously reported membranes have fluxes much larger than that of the MOF-801-based membranes reported in this manuscript (maximum reported flux in this manuscript of ~38 L m-2 h-1).
Unlike in say, for example, pressure driven reverse osmosis desalination membranes, by the inherent nature of transport through the pervaporation process the flux of the pervaporation desalination membranes is largely insensitive to the feed concentration. This is because the driving force is not proportional to the difference between the applied pressure and the osmotic pressure of the feed solution (which is significantly reduced for hypersaline feed solutions), but the driving force in pervaporation is a function of the chemical potential difference, which is practically realized in the pervaporation process as a vapor pressure difference… and it is well established that the vapor pressure of the saline feed solutions does not change significantly as a function of solute concentration because the vapor pressure of salts is essentially negligible at any potential operational temperature of pervaporation. The vapor pressure differential, therefore, obviously is increased by either increasing the feed solution temperature or decreasing the permeate side vacuum level.
This manuscript also fails to report the water permeation results in the standard parameter preferred in the membrane science community – permeance (or permeability). The authors are referred to the excellent paper “Permeability, permeance and selectivity: A preferred way of reporting pervaporation performance data” by Richard W. Baker et al. ttps://doi.org/10.1016/j.memsci.2009.11.022 to understand the standard convention and include them in their updated resubmission to an alternate journal.
Finally, the use of a molecule (in this case the surfactant/zwitterion Span80) to backfill defects in cracks of an inorganic membrane structure is not novel.
Overall, this manuscript fails to recognize the extensive body of literature on pervaporation desalination, does not use standard conventions for reporting permeance in pervaporation membranes, and the reported membranes do not have such outstanding performance properties. While this paper may have some interesting materials science aspects to it and modeling components, the potential impact of these beyond the small field of pervaporation desalination is not sufficient to justify publication in Nature Communications.

### Reviewer 3

Polycrystalline MOF membranes have shown great potential for molecular separation. Most current works focus on removing inter-granular defects (e.g., cracks) to obtain continuous MOF membrane.
There are few reports paying attention to the lattice defects in MOF membrane. This manuscript focuses on the precise regulation of missing linkers lattice defects in MOF-801 membrane by controlling the amount of modulator for pervaporation desalination, which is novel. The relationship between the lattice defects and membrane microstructure was systematically investigated, and outstanding desalination was achieved owing to the missing linkers enhance membrane structural hydrophilicity with stronger host-guest interaction energy. The idea to precisely control lattice defects by simply adjusting the amount of modulator is interesting, which would inspire fabricating other next-generation MOF nanochannel membranes with high separation performance. Therefore, the manuscript can be accepted by the journal, however, several issues should be further addressed.
1.In view of the topic “Lattice-defects engineering in MOF membrane for desalination”, the authors are suggested to give a comparison between this work with the highly relevant recent paper (Nat. Mater. 2023, 22, 769). In addition, the proposed in situ nano-seeding strategy to construct MOF-801 membrane in this work was also reported by the same authors for preparing another type of Zr-MOF membranes, UiO-66 membrane (Nat. Common. 2022, 13, 266), what is the essential difference between the two works, the authors should further clarify it.
2.When the evaporation takes place, salts ions cannot be vaporized and the presence of membrane would inevitably increase the transfer resistance during the pervaporation desalination process. The membrane distillation (MD) is very similar to pervaporation desalination. MD uses the low-grade waste heat, not vacuum that is one of the most expensive form of energy. What is the advantage of pervaporation desalination compared with MD?
3.What is the role of TiO2 layer for membrane formation? If without TiO2, can the continuous MOF membrane be prepared by the in-situ nano-seeding strategy followed by surfactant post-treatment?
4.The authors tried to post-treat MOF membrane using three kinds of surfactants, SLS, DTAB, and Span 80. Results show that only Span 80 facilitates the formation of cracks-free membrane (Fig.1 and Fig. S7). Why? The authors are suggested to provide the detailed explanation.
5.The authors stated “Ti was detected in the TiO2 nano-interlayer surface, while only Zr was detected in the crack-free MOF-801 membrane surface, suggesting the intergrowth integrity of the membrane”, I am very curious why the Zr was not detected in cracked MOF-801 membrane shown in Fig. S11, because lots of MOF crystals were also deposited in substrate surface (Fig. 1b), the signal of Zr should be significant. According to the description by the authors, in Fig. S11, the icon a2 should be cracked-free MOF-801 membrane.

## Paper

## Abstract

We report a method for the precise regulation of intracrystalline missing-linkers to control the
permeability and selectivity of metal-organic framework (MOF) membranes. The method is
applied for the design of stable ceramic-based MOF-801 membranes for hypersaline water
treatment via pervaporation. For efficient membrane growth, an in situ nano-seeding strategy was
employed to provide nucleation sites followed by surfactant posttreatment to minimize cracks.
Missing-linkers are regulated in MOF-801 membranes by altering the ratio of fumarate to formic
acid, which positively enhances water transport by modifying the MOF-801 structure and
chemistry. Specifically, missing-linkers enhance membrane structural hydrophilicity with stronger
host-guest interaction energy, resulting in faster transport with a lower energy barrier by enlarging
the pore window and pore cage. The MOF-801 membranes demonstrated near-perfect salt
rejection (~99.9%) and high water flux, outperform most state-of-the-art silica, MOF, and
zeolite polycrystalline membranes for the treatment of both saline and hypersaline waters. Notably,
the membranes exhibited stable desalination performance, highlighting their promising application
potential. This work provides a strategy for the rational design of next-generation high-
performance MOF nanochannel membranes for challenging water purification applications.

---

## Introduction

To combat global water scarcity, desalination will play a critical role in tapping into
unconventional water sources.1,2 While reverse osmosis (RO) is the current paradigm for
desalination, conventional RO cannot be used for hypersaline waters (salinity > ~10 wt.%) due to
the ultrahigh osmotic pressures that must be overcome, which exceed the maximum hydraulic
pressures that can be applied.3-6 At these higher salinities, thermally-driven membrane processes
have an advantage over RO as their operation is less sensitive to salinity.7-9 A promising chemical-
potential-driven membrane process is pervaporation (PV).10 A liquid feed stream (heated in some
cases) is exposed to one side of the PV membrane and a vacuum is applied to the other. Under
these conditions, water traverses the PV membrane, vaporizes, and then condensed at the permeate
side.9,11,12 In this process, dissolved salts are retained because salts, unlike water, have negligible
vapor pressure at the operational temperatures and pressures of pervaporation. PV is capable of
treating hypersaline waters, even when operated at ambient temperatures.13,14 Unlike conventional
membrane distillation (MD) processes, a more robust PV process has advantages in addressing
challenges like wetting, scaling, and fouling, which enables promising operational performance.15

A major challenge for PV desalination is the design of high-performance separation
membranes featuring high permeability, salt rejection, and operating stability.9,16,17 Unlike their
polymer counterparts, more robust inorganic polycrystalline nanoporous membranes, such as
zeolite and silica, have been proposed.18,19 While these membranes offered stable desalination
performance, they suffered from low permeability, even for the treatment of seawater or low-
salinity wastewaters. In contrast, metal-organic framework (MOF) membranes have well-defined
nanochannel structures, abundant affinity sites, modular nature for functionalities, and structural
stability, thereby enabling high uptake of water and promising separation performance.20-23
Compared with state-of-the-art water-stable MOFs, MOF-801 demonstrates highly robust
characteristics, rapid water adsorption rate, and high water harvesting capacity.24-28 In addition,
MOF-801 inherently possesses a suitable crystallographic structure where the pore window size
(3.5 Å) ranges between water molecules (2.8 Å) and hydrated sodium ions (~ 7.16 Å). This makes
MOF-801 a promising candidate for desalination membranes with precise separation ability, which
has not been experimentally demonstrated until now. However, the fabrication of a well-
intergrown (i.e., crack-free or intercrystalline-defect-free) pure MOF-801 membrane is
experimentally difficult and thus lags behind its mixed-matrix membrane and other MOF
membrane counterparts.

Rational tailoring of crystalline chemistry of MOF membranes has the potential to
substantially improve membrane functionality and performance, but is considered to be
particularly challenging. Recently, intracrystalline defects, such as missing linkers and missing
clusters, have been synthesized and confirmed to influence the permeability or selectivity of MOF
liquid- or gas-separation membranes.29-33 However, the precise creation of favorable
intracrystalline defects is challenging and has not been well-studied in membrane-based separation
applications. Moreover, it remains unclear how intracrystalline missing linkers affect separation
performance, such as selectivity and permeability, at the molecular or atomic level. Therefore,
elucidating these transport mechanisms is critical for the rational design of nanoscale channels
with tailorable structure and chemistry in next-generation MOF membranes. Unlike the
elimination of intracrystalline lattice defects to improve the selectivity of MOF membranes 27, the
aim of this work is to precisely regulate intracrystalline missing linkers of MOF membranes to
enhance the permeation of water molecules while maintaining high salt rejection. Differing from
a former study that introduced an arbitrary number of missing linkers (~23.5%),30 this work
demonstrates that precise regulation of missing linkers to enhance water transport could be realized
in MOF-801 membranes, which is not only practically challenging, but also critical for
understanding fundamental mass transport phenomena.

In this work, we report a robust protocol for well-intergrown MOF-801 nanochannel thin
membranes with precise regulation of intracrystalline missing linkers for enhanced water
permeability via pervaporation. We further provide a mechanistic understanding of the missing-
linker enhancement of water permeation, where missing linkers not only enhance structural
hydrophilicity (i.e., water adsorption ability) but also render faster water transport via altering the
pore structure and chemistry of the nanoscale MOF-801 channels. The membranes exhibit
complete salt rejection, operation stability, and higher water flux in comparison to state-of-the-art
silica, MOF, and zeolite membranes for the treatment of saline and hypersaline waters. Notably,
the MOF-801 membranes demonstrated resilient performance under challenging water treatment
conditions, including high temperatures, highly oxidizing environments, and in the presence of
oils and surfactants.

---

## Results

Design and Characterization of Crack-free MOF-801 Membrane
Engineering the structure and surface properties of substrates is crucial for subsequent MOF
membrane growth and application. In this work, crack-free MOF-801 membranes were fabricated
by a secondary growth method followed by surfactant Span80 posttreatment for PV desalination
(Figure 1, Supplementary Figures 1-3). Ceramic substrates (α-Al2O3:average pore size ~700 nm;
ZrO2: average pore size ~ 142 nm) were specially designed with a hollow fiber configuration for
PV, featuring an ultrahigh packing density (~4000 m2·m-3) that is 16-40 times higher than those of
tubular (200-250 m2·m-3) or flat-sheet (100-150 m2·m-3) commercial substrates; with the latter
most commonly used as the substrate for current MOF membranes (Figure 1a, Supplementary
Figure 4, SI Section 1.2).34 To modify the substrate and enable the growth of well-intergrown
MOF-801 membranes, a more hydrophilic nano-TiO2 interlayer was introduced with lowered
surface roughness (Ra ~68 nm) (Supplementary Figure 4) and average pore size (~105 nm). Such
a TiO2 interlayer could provide a modified substrate surface with more hydroxyl groups and thus
more nucleation sites for MOF crystal nucleation and subsequent growth, which is beneficial to
the formation of thin, well-intergrown MOF-801 membranes. MOF-801 was selected to be
fabricated into a separation membrane because of its stability toward some solvents, especially
hypersaline solutions at elevated temperatures (Supplementary Figure 5). Although there were
only minor and negligible additional peaks for the samples after exposure in DMF, acetone, and
water—the phase structure degraded to some extent in strongly acidic aqueous solution (pH 0.7),
which can be reflected by peak broadening and new peaks arising (Supplementary Figure 5).
Nevertheless, such chemically harsh condition is far beyond practical application conditions. In
this work, a nanoseed-induced secondary growth method (seed size: ~69 nm, Supplementary
Figure 6) was employed to fabricate the polycrystalline MOF-801 membrane to increase the
presence of active nucleation sites and reduce the energy barrier for nucleation based on Ostwald’s
rule.35

One key challenge is the generation of macroscopic cracks inside MOF-801 membranes during
drying after membrane growth (Figures 1a, 1b), which inevitably undermines the separation
performance. To address this issue, a surfactant (Span80) posttreatment was employed to
effectively avoid the formation of cracks (Figures 1a, 1c, Supplementary Figure 7). For the
polycrystalline MOF-801 membrane, cracks formed due to the increased capillary stress between
intergrown MOF crystals during the solvent evaporation stage.36 However, after being soaked in a
Span80 chloroform solution for 2 days, high-quality MOF-801 membranes (thickness ~1.67 μm)
with a pure MOF-801 phase were obtained on a TiO2 interlayer-modified ceramic substrate with
visible and distinct boundaries (Figures 1d, 1g), which were free of macroscopic intracrystalline
cracks (Figure 1c). Posttreatment of the MOF-801 membrane with Span80 significantly
suppressed the evaporation rate of residual solvents (N,N-dimethyl formamide, formic acid) and
reduced capillary stress, consequently minimizing the formation of cracks. Unlike the unmodified
MOF-801 membrane (“cracked”), which exhibits poor gas selectivity, the modified MOF-801
membrane is well-intergrown (i.e., without macroscopic cracks or other intercrystalline defects)
since its ideal gas selectivities (H2/N2: 7.6, H2/CH4: 16.5, N2/CH4: 2.2) are all higher than the
Knudsen diffusion selectivities (H2/N2: 3.7, H2/CH4: 2.8, N2/CH4: 1.3) (Figure 1e).

The ATR-FTIR spectrum of the modified MOF-801 membrane verifies the presence of the -
C=O-O bond (1400 cm-1, 1577 cm-1) and -C=O-OH group (1213 cm-1) of the MOF-801
structure,37,38 as well as the in-plane deformation vibration of C-H (2852-2856 cm-1, 2921−2925
cm-1) and strong stretching vibration of ester bonds (1734−1742 cm -1) of the Span80 structure
(Figure 1f).39 Nevertheless, Span80 posttreatment did not significantly change the pore size (6 Å
vs. 6 Å) and specific surface area (499 m2·g-1 vs. 535.5 m2·g-1) of MOF-801 (Supplementary Figure
8), which indicates that such a surfactant posttreatment modification would not negatively affect
the pore structure of the membranes. Additionally, the presence of O, Ti, Zr, and C signals in the
XPS spectra are clearly identified for the TiO2 interlayer, cracked MOF-801, and crack-free MOF-
801 membranes (Supplementary Figure 9). Ti was detected in the TiO2
nano-interlayer surface,
while Zr was detected in the membrane surface of both cracked and crack-free MOF-801
membranes (Supplementary Figures 9, 10). Moreover, even after strong ultrasonication treatment
(150 W, 20 min) for an accelerated stability test, the MOF-801-1.43 membrane maintained
integrated surface and cross-sectional structural morphologies, indicating promising mechanical
stability for practical operation Supplementary Figure 11).

Precise Regulation of Intracrystalline Missing Linkers
Although missing linkers have been experimentally designed in UiO-66 MOF membranes,
precise regulation of intracrystalline missing linkers has not been reported until now.32 Without the
addition of a modulator, it is difficult to form highly crystalline MOF-801 membrane (usually only
some amorphous phase) from ZrOCl2 and fumarate due to the slow crystallization kinetics.40 The
amorphous phase on substrates is not suitable for pervaporation desalination since it does not form
a membrane layer with defined MOF crystalline structure comprised of regular pore window and
pore cage to allow for water molecule transport and salt rejection. By contrast, our current work,
employs formic acid as a modulator to not only accelerate the crystallization of MOF-801, but also
precisely regulate intracrystalline missing linkers by adjusting the ratio of fumarate to formic acid
(Figure 2, Supplementary Figure 12). The intracrystalline missing linkers were first identified and
quantified based on the results of X-Ray diffraction (XRD), 1H Nuclear Magnetic Resonance
(NMR), 13C Magic Angle Spinning (MAS) NMR, and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) (Figures
2b-2e, Supplementary Figures 13-15). By adjusting the ratios of fumarate to formic acid (10:400,
6:400, 4:400, 2:400 and 1:400), the frequency of missing linkers per Zr6 crystalline formula unit
(denoted as linker deficiency unless specified) can be precisely regulated and was determined to
be 0.32, 0.70, 1.25, 1.43, and 1.62, based on the TGA results (denoted as MOF-801-0.32, MOF-
801-0.70, MOF-801-1.25, MOF-801-1.43, and MOF-801-1.62 in this work) (Figure 2b).

The TGA results indicated that a deficiency was present in all samples due to deviations in
mass loss behavior in comparison to the ideal plateau of MOF-801 (Supplementary Figure 13).41
The presence of missing clusters were ruled out according to the XRD patterns where no reo phase
was observed between 2 and 8° (2θ) (Figure 2c).42 Therefore, we can conclude that the
intracrystalline defects are the result of missing linkers. In addition to fumarate molecules, the
presence of HCOO- (formic molecule) can be experimentally confirmed by the 1H NMR spectra
(Figure 2d), indicating the occurrence of a competitive coordination reaction between the Zr6
cluster and formic acid. This can be ascribed to the fact that during the solvothermal reaction,
formic acid coordinates with Zr6 clusters via carboxyl groups by competing with fumarate acid to
form the missing fumarate linkers.

With increasing missing-linker density, the pore structure of MOF-801 was enlarged, which
was confirmed by the near-linear increase in pore size (i.e., pore width, from 4.62 to 5.09 Å), total
pore volume (from 0.36 to 0.68 cm-3∙g-1), and specific surface area (from 292.1 to 791.1 m-2∙g-1)
(Figures 2e, 2f, Supplementary Figure 14). Moreover, the water uptake capacity was enhanced
with the increasing presence of missing linkers (Figure 2f), which is not only a result of the
enlarged pore structure but also the generation of more hydrophilic sites with enhanced water
adsorption ability. For the pervaporation desalination process (Supplementary Figure 3), the
presence of missing linkers reduced the activation energy barrier required for water molecule
transport across the membranes (Supplementary Figure 16). Furthermore, the water flux of MOF-
801 membranes linearly increased with increasing linker deficiency under constant operational
temperatures (40-80℃), while salt rejection remains nearly complete, in the range of 99.69% -
99.91% under all operational temperatures (Figure 2g). Specifically, when the linker deficiency
increases from 0.32 to 1.43, the water flux is enhanced by ~60% at 80℃. Additionally, increasing
the operational temperature from 40 to 80℃ improves the water flux from 12.3 to 35.6 L∙m-2∙h-1
at a 1.43 linker deficiency due to the enhanced driving force. The performance of the membrane
with the highest linker deficiency 1.62 is not shown since it was synthesized under strongly acidic
conditions, resulting in poor membrane quality and desalination performance.

Atomistic Mechanism for Missing-Linker Enhanced Performance
To shed light on the effect of missing linkers on desalination performance, state-of-the-art
molecular simulations, including molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo, associated with
experimental data were employed to offer atomistic insights into the permeation mechanism of
water molecules through MOF-801 membranes (Figure 3, SI Section 3.1). To reveal the role of
missing linkers, we investigated a defect-free simulation structure and two highly symmetric
missing-linker simulation structures with theoretical deficiency of 1/12 and 1/4 (also denoted
MOF-801-DF, MOF-801-0.5, and MOF-801-1.5, respectively). Through these simulations, the
improvement in water flux was ascribed to missing linkers not only enhancing water adsorption
(i.e., water affinity) but also water transport by altering the intracrystalline pore microenvironment
(i.e., more hydrophilic active sites) and structure (i.e., both enlarged pore window and pore cage)
of the subnanometer channels in the MOF-801 framework structure. Reducing the activation
energy barrier, the presence of missing linkers enables the ultrafast transport of more water
molecules (Figures 3a−3e). Missing linkers also enhance the structural hydrophilicity of the MOF
frameworks due to the exposure of more water adsorption sites (i.e., [Zr6(OH)4O4] cluster),
resulting in a higher water uptake rate and higher water loading (Figures 3f, 3g, SI Section 3.2).

To gain insight into such an enhancement from an energetic point of view, Monte Carlo
simulations were conducted to sample the interaction energy between a single water molecule and
MOF-801 framework structures. The interaction energy distribution for MOF-801-0.5 and MOF-
801-1.5 indicated stronger interactions resulting from water-framework Coulombic interactions
when compared to MOF-801-DF (Figure 3h). As a result, MOF-801 exhibited 4-16 times higher
adsorption capacity when compared with other state-of-the-art, water-stable MOFs (i.e., ML-UiO-
66, UiO-66, UiO-66-NH2) (Figure 3i). During the PV process, the creation of more missing linkers
enhances the permeation dynamics of more water molecules inside the membranes (Figure 3j).
Theoretically, the water flux significantly increases from 16.4 to 36.4 L·m−1·h−1 with increasing
missing linker deficiency from 0 to 1.5 (Figure 3k). We can, therefore, conclude that
intracrystalline missing linkers in the MOF-801 membrane not only promote the structural
hydrophilicity (i.e., water adsorption ability) but also render faster transport dynamics (i.e.,
diffusion ability) of water molecules. These two aspects result in the higher water flux of MOF-
801 membranes with more missing linkers than was observed experimentally. As previously noted,
the MOF-801-1.62 membrane synthesized under strongly acidic conditions exhibit poor
desalination performance. Thus, the high-quality MOF-801-1.43 membrane was selected for
subsequent performance and stability evaluation and will be referred to as MOF-801 membrane
unless specified hereafter.

Promising Desalination Performance and Operation Stability
The MOF-801 membranes exhibited exceptional desalination performance and operation
stability for the treatment of saline waters in a wide range of concentrations (0-10 wt.% NaCl)
(Figure 4). Independent of salt concentration and operation temperature, the rejection of all MOF-
801 membranes are over 99.9%, resulting in permeate salt concentrations of 2-44 ppm, which are
lower than the product water quality standards of both China and the WHO for desalination
techniques (China HY/T 247-2018: 50 ppm (salt concentration), WHO: 1,200 ppm (total dissolved
solids)) (Supplementary Figure 17).9 This performance indicates that the MOF-801 membranes
could effectively desalinate brines to produce clean water by PV (Figures 4a, S3). The pore size of
MOF-801-1.43 was determined to be 5.07 Å (Figure 2d, Supplementary Figure 14b), which is
lower than the size of hydrated ions (d [Na+·(H2O)n] ~ 0.716 nm, d [Cl-·(H2O)n] ~ 0.664 nm).43
The near-complete salt rejections could be ascribed to the fact that the salt ions have negligible
vapor pressure at the operating conditions, and did not vaporize in the pervaporation process.

In particular, even at approximately room temperature (30°C) (without heat energy input on the
feed side), water flux is still very promising (e.g., 6.3 Lm-2·h-1 for 3.5 wt.% saline water, 3.9 Lm-
2·h-1 for 10 wt.% hypersaline water) (Figure 4a). This energy-saving feature is different from the
MD process, where the water flux (~1 Lm-2·h-1) is often negligible at room temperature.54 For
saline waters with the same concentration, water flux was further enhanced with operation
temperature (from 30 to 70°C) due to an enhanced driving force of the adsorption-diffusion process
of water molecules, since PV is a typical thermal activation adsorption-diffusion process.49 The
activation energy (Eact.) is approximately 3.69 kJ·mol−1 for 3.5 wt.% saline water (Supplementary
Figure 17), which is less than those of other PV processes.49 At the same operating temperature,
the water flux was demonstrated to show a declining trend with increasing feed salt concentration
(Figure 4a).50 This phenomenon is attributed to the elevated salt concentration at the vaporization
interface, where fewer free water molecules are transported across the MOF-801 membrane
because more water molecules are bound to salt ions to form a hydration shell. Moreover, the
MOF-801-1.43 membrane showed high water flux (27.4 Lm-2·h-1) for treating saline waters (3.5
wt.% NaCl), outperforming most state-of-the-art silica, zeolite, and MOF membranes (1-10 Lm-
2·h-1) (Figure 4b). Unlike other studies focusing on 3.5 wt.% NaCl saline water treatment, the
MOF-801 membrane exhibited promising water flux (10.5 Lm-2·h-1) for even more challenging
hypersaline waters (10 wt.%), which are 1.6–7.4 times that of current zeolite and MOF membranes
(Figure 4c). Like the water flux, the water permeance of the MOF-801 membranes were enhanced
with linker deficiencies but decreased with salt concentration (Supplementary Figure 18).

Differentiating from most other MOF membranes that suffer from insufficient water stability,
MOF-801 membranes demonstrate stable operational performance (in both flux and rejection) and
acceptable structural integrity (in both MOF-801 crystalline phase and membrane morphology)
for the treatment of 7 wt.% hypersaline water at 70°C for 120 h (Figures 4d, 4f, 4 g).55 Under XRD,
the MOF-801 membranes exhibited two characteristic reflections of MOF-801 phase between 7
and 11° before and after operation, indicating some stability in their phase crystalline structure
(Figure 4f). However, some peak width broadening was found from 0.24 to 0.37 especially after
108 h exposure at pH 3, which reflected a change in the lattice structure to some extent (i.e., crystal
lattice grain sizes might decrease slightly), while the peaks were nearly unchanged in the case of
hypersaline water exposure. The efficient treatment of harsh environmental wastewaters can be
challenging for conventional membranes. However, after soaking in an acidic hypersaline solution
(pH=3, 10 wt % NaCl), the MOF-801 membrane still exhibited stable flux and salt rejection over
~100 h of operation (Figure 4e). Even after constant operation in harsh environments (e.g., high
temperature, high salinity, and low pH ∼3), the MOF-801 membrane showed good structural
integrity, which was confirmed by its resilient surface morphology, phase composition, and high
ideal gas selectivity (Figures 4f, 4g, Supplementary Figure 19). These results indicate that MOF-
801 membranes are promising candidates for the production of clean water from hypersaline brines
via PV.

To further investigate the resilience of the MOF-801 membrane, desalination performance and
operation stability were evaluated under harsh treatment conditions using acidic brines, industrial
wastewaters, and oxidizing brines (Figure 5). Acidic hypersaline waters with an initial pH of 3
could be concentrated to the point of crystallization by using MOF-801 membranes at an operating
temperature of 70℃, all while consistently producing pure water on the permeate side of the
membrane (Figure 5a, Supplementary Figure 20). During operation, the water flux gradually
decreased from 10.5 to 2.6 Lm-2·h-1 due to the decreasing driving force caused by the feed being
concentrated 4.45-fold, all while salt rejection was maintained above 99.9%.

The treatment of real industrial acidic saline wastewater (pH ~3.4) can also be challenging for
conventional membranes because of its complicated composition (Supplementary Table 5).
Interestingly, the MOF-801 membrane exhibits promisingly stable performance under these
conditions (Figure 5b). The water flux first decreased from its initial value of ~ 10.4 L m–2 h–1 and
then remained relatively stable in the range of ~ 5.0 – 6.0 L m–2 h–1due to the membrane fouling
at the vaporization interface (i.e., membrane surface). By using a simple DI water cleaning method,
the water flux of the MOF-801 membranes could be efficiently recovered to 9.85 L m–2 h–1 (with
a recovery ratio of ~ 94%). In addition to having a stable water flux, the membrane shows high
rejection of all salt ions, such as Na+, K+, Mg2+, and Ca2+ (all above 99.0%), which can be ascribed
to that fact that salt ions have negligible vapor pressure, and did not vaporize during the
pervaporation process.

One of the major challenges for conventional polyamide membranes is their susceptibility to
chlorine oxidation.56 Unlike polyamide membranes, the MOF-801 membranes showed a highly
stable desalination performance for hypersaline water feed even at 70℃ after exposure to 100 ppm
NaClO aqueous solution for as long as 21 days (i.e., equivalent to 50,400 ppm·h chlorine exposure)
(Figure 5c); indicating a significantly improved chlorine resistance (1.7 – 20.0 times higher) than
both commercial and state-of-the-art polyamide membranes (2,500 – 30,430 ppm·h chlorine
exposure).57,58 After continuous operation under these different extreme conditions, all the MOF-
801 membranes retained their integrity as exhibited by the ideal selectivities of H2/N2 gases, which
were still higher than their Knudsen diffusion selectivity (H2/N2: 3.7) (Figure 5f, Supplementary
Figure 21). Moreover, the MOF-801 membranes exhibited stability in both the crystalline phase
and membrane structure, which is reflected by the XRD (only except for slight peak-width
broadening), 1H NMR spectra, ATR-FTIR spectra, and membrane surface morphology (Figures
5d, 5e, 5g, 5h). The performance stability can be ascribed to the highly stable membrane structure
consisting of well intergrown MOF-801 crystals in which there are highly robust Zr–O covalent
bonds, and strong coordination bonds between [Zr6(OH)4O4] cluster (i.e., Lewis acid) and
fumarate linker (i.e., Lewis base). Additionally, unlike commercial polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)
distillation membranes (Nanjing CAS-Bidun Newmen Technology Co., Ltd., China), the MOF-
801 pervaporation membranes show better desalination performance and operating stability for
treating more challenging hypersaline waters containing low surface tension species, including oil
and surfactant (Supplementary Figure 22). This is similar to what was previously reported between
commercial PTFE distillation membranes and polymeric pervaporation membranes.59 This
resilient desalination performance under various harsh conditions indicates the application
potential of the robust MOF-801 membranes in a wide range of industrial applications.

## Methods

In situ Synthesis of MOF-801 Nanoseed Layer
Both Al2O3 and ZrO2 ceramic substrates (100-200 pieces for each membrane) were first fabricated
by an immersion-induced phase inversion process, followed by complete drying and sintering at
1550°C for 4 h (Al2O3) or at 1050°C for 2 h (ZrO2). A TiO2 interlayer was then coated onto the
substrates by a dip-coating method, followed by complete drying and sintering at 800°C for 4 h.
Then, a thin layer of uniformly dispersed MOF-801 nanoseeds (size ~69 nm) was synthesized in
situ on the outer surface of TiO2 interlayer-modified ceramic substrates via the solvothermal
method. Specifically, fumaric acid and ZrOCl2·8H2O were first dissolved into a solvent mixture
of DMF and formic acid. Then, the substrates with both sides sealed were placed into the mixture
solution inside a 100 mL Teflon reactor for the solvothermal reaction at 120°C for 24 h to form a
MOF-801 nanoseed layer in situ. Finally, after the reaction was allowed to cool, the samples were
cleaned with DMF.

Preparation of Crack-free MOF-801 Membrane
MOF-801 membranes with different missing linkers (10-20 pieces for each membrane
composition) were synthesized via a solvothermal secondary growth method, followed by
surfactant posttreatment. To create different missing-linker densities, fumaric acid (0.1420 g,
0.4260 g, 0.7087 g) and formic acid (9 mL) at different molar ratios (fumaric acid: formic acid =
2:400, 6:400, 10:400) were first mixed with DMF (61 mL) and ZrOCl2·8H2O (0.4025 g). Then,
the substrates coated with a MOF-801 nanoseed layer were placed into the mixture solution inside
a 100 mL Teflon reactor for solvothermal reaction at 120°C for 24 h to allow for the secondary
growth of MOF-801 membranes. Finally, after the reaction, the MOF-801 membranes were
cleaned with DMF and dried at room temperature for 6 h to produce the cracked MOF-801
membranes. To avoid the formation of cracks, the synthesized MOF-801 membranes were
immediately immersed into a Span80 solution (1 g Span80 dissolved in 10 mL chloroform) for 24
h prior to drying. The MOF-801 membranes were completely dried in a chloroform atmosphere
for 72 h and then activated to remove any solvent molecules (DMF) at 150°C for 24 h under
vacuum (-1 bar).

Membrane Performance Evaluation
The desalination performance of MOF-801 membranes (effective membrane area ~100-200 mm2)
was evaluated in a lab-scale pervaporation (PV) setup with various saline waters (1.5, 3.5, 7 wt. %
NaCl, pH 7), hypersaline water (10 wt.% NaCl, pH 7), acidic hypersaline water (10 wt.% NaCl,
pH 3), and real industrial acidic saline wastewater (A machinery factory, Dalian City, Liaoning
Province, China) as the feeds (feed water reservoir volume ~100-250 ml) (Supplementary Figure
3). The pervaporation system was first stabilized for ~2 h. The feed flow rate was controlled at 160
±5 mL min–1 by a peristaltic pump, while a vacuum of (~60 Pa) was applied on the permeate side.
A cold trap was utilized to cool and collect the permeate water after condensation at different time
intervals (~2h). The permeate flux (Jw, L·m-2·h-1) was determined at a certain time interval (Δt, h)
based on the volume of the condensed permeate (ΔV, L) across a constant effective membrane area
(A, m2) according to Eq. (1). During membrane operation, the salt concentration of the solution
was measured using a conductivity meter (DDSJ-308A, Shanghai REX Instrument Factory, China).
The conductivity of the feed solution was used to calculate the salt concentration based on a
calibration curve. Salt rejection was determined according to Eq. 2, where Cf (mg·L−1) and Cp
(mg·L−1) are the salt concentrations of the permeate and feed, respectively:

Jw = ΔV / (A * Δt) (1)
R = (Cf - Cp) / Cf (2)

Molecular Simulations
Classical molecular dynamics simulations, implemented in the LAMMPS package, were
conducted to investigate the pervaporation desalination mechanism of MOF-801-DF, MOF-801-
0.5, and MOF-801-1.5 membranes.60 The simulation system and results are described in detail in
SI Section 3 (Supplementary Figures 23,24).

Pervaporation simulations were carried out in a canonical ensemble (i.e., NVT) at a temperature
of 343 K with a time step of 1 fs. The system’s temperature was modulated using the Nosé‒Hoover
thermostat with a damping factor of 100 time steps (i.e., 100 fs). For each simulation, energy
minimization was first carried out to preliminarily relax the system. Subsequently, a hydrostatic
pressure of 1 atm was applied on the feed pistons, and a molecular dynamics simulation was
performed for 40 ns to bring the liquid density closer to its equilibrium value (i.e., 1.0 g cm−3) and
to fully saturate the initially empty membrane structure with saline solution. Finally, the systems
were further equilibrated for 5 ps, followed by a production run of 20 ps at a constant pressure of
1 atm. We should note that all of the studied membranes, as well as the piston and adsorbing plate,
were assumed to be rigid.

Characterization
The structural morphology or element composition of MOF-801 membranes and ceramic
substrates were characterized in a field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM) (S-4800,
Hitachi, Japan; NOVA NanoSEM 450, FEI Company, USA) equipped with an energy dispersive
spectrometer (EDS). X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements were carried out in an Ultima IV X-
ray diffractometer using Cu-Kα radiation with a step size of 0.02° and 2 s per step (D/Max-2400,
Rigaku, Japan). The functional groups of the MOF-801 membrane and powder were analyzed by
attenuated total reflectance-Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR) (IS50, Thermo
Nicolet, US). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was used for analysis of elements using a
Thermo Fisher K-Alpha spectrometer (K-Alpha, Thermo Fisher, USA). Thermogravimetric
analysis (TGA) was carried out in a thermal analyzer (TG/DTA 6300, Seiko Co., Ltd., Japan) at a
heating rate of 5°C min-1 from room temperature (~25℃) to 700°C in air. Liquid 1H nuclear
magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra were recorded in a nuclear magnetic resonance spectrometer
(Bruker Advance Ⅲ500, Bruker, Switzerland). The nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherms of
MOF-801 crystals were recorded in an automatic physical adsorption apparatus (AS-1-MP-11,
Quantachrome, USA). Dynamic vapor sorption (DVS, Surface Measurement System Ltd., UK)
was used to measure the water uptake behaviors of MOF-801 and Span80-posttreated MOF-801
crystals, as well as UiO-66 and UiO-66-NH2.

Other detailed characterization can be found in the Supplementary Materials (SI Section 1.4).

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript reports a novel approach to enhancing the permeability and selectivity of MOF-801 membranes through the precise regulation of intracrystalline missing-linker defects, which is a significant contribution to the field of water desalination technology. The method of employing an in situ nano-seeding strategy alongside surfactant post-treatment to minimize crack formation represents a notable advance in MOF membrane fabrication. The research's innovation is further underscored by its application to hypersaline water treatment via pervaporation, demonstrating exceptional performance metrics, including near-perfect salt rejection (~99.8%) and high water flux (12.3 L∙m^-2∙h^-1 at 40℃), setting a new standard in the field.
The authors should consider the following concerns:

What specific interactions at the molecular level lead to enhanced water transport and selectivity? A more rigorous theoretical framework or simulation data supporting these claims is suggested.
2. Control group comparisons: While the performance improvements are highlighted, the manuscript does not provide a detailed comparison with control groups lacking the precise regulation of missing-linker defects. How does the performance of unmodified MOF-801 membranes compare, and what is the quantitative impact of your innovations?
