Important novel aspects are described below:
1. The first novel aspect in this work is the precise regulation of missing linkers lattice
defects in the MOF membrane (Fig. 2). Intracrystalline defects—such as missing linkers and
missing clusters—have been synthesized and confirmed to influence the permeability or
selectivity of MOF liquid- or gas-separation membranes. However, the precise regulation of
favorable intracrystalline defects and their effect on fundamental mass transport phenomena
for desalination has not been previously reported for membrane-based separation applications.
As Reviewer #3 positively commented in the last round of review, there are few reports
paying attention to the lattice defects in MOF membranes. More importantly, we
demonstrated a facile method to precisely control the frequency of missing linkers, which has
not been previously realized for MOF membranes.
2. The second novel aspect is the characterization of the atomistic mechanism for
enhanced water transport induced by precise regulation of missing linkers (Fig. 3).
While published works on pervaporation desalination largely focus on membrane fabrication
and performance evaluation, very rarely is the fundamental atomistic mechanism for water
transport explored. Interestingly, we found that precise regulation of missing linkers enhances
membrane structural hydrophilicity with stronger host-guest interaction energy. Resulting in a
lower energy barrier by enlarging the MOF pore window and pore cage, the structural
configuration of MOF-801 with the precise regulation of missing linkers enables the observed
increase in water flux. We strongly believe this fundamental understanding has broader
scientific implications and will aid in bridging knowledge gaps across different disciplines
and fields of science, technology, and engineering (e.g., chemistry, materials, environmental
science, chemical engineering, water and membrane technologies). Thus, we believe that this
work with fundamental mechanistic insights is of great interest for the broad readership of
Nature Communications.

in comparison to other state-of-the-art zeolite and MOF membranes for pervaporation
desalination. As you have recognized, our work is the first report to use the
material MOF-801 for pervaporation desalination and has some interesting materials
science aspects and modeling components. We recognize that some pervaporation desalination
membranes—especially polymeric membranes—have higher performance (with respect to
water flux) under specific conditions, but we wish to emphasize that our MOF membranes
indeed outperform state-of-the-art zeolite and MOF membranes in water flux (Figure 4 and
Tables S5-6), which belong to an emerging class of polycrystalline molecular sieve
membranes that are drastically different from polymeric membranes (such as PVA
membranes). As a result, the performance comparison of membranes with similar structures
and properties was deemed more appropriate for this study.

conditions (i.e., high-temperature, acidic, oxidizing conditions, feeds with refractory species
like oil or surfactants) of our MOF membrane. Differing from previous reports focusing on
desalination under mild conditions, we intentionally subjected our MOF membrane to harsh
chemical conditions for prolonged periods of time to evaluate their resilience in practical
applications that have proven challenging for conventional polymeric membranes (Fig. 4, Fig.
5, Fig. S16-21, Table S4). To this end, our MOF membrane showcased stable performance
when treating real industrial wastewater with a complicated composition, which has not
been successfully demonstrated previously (Fig. 5, Table S4). Stable operation under harsh
chemical conditions is of great practical significance for membrane technologies. We believe
that this has broader implications for the design and synthesis of novel membrane materials
(e.g., MOF-801 in our work), which has not been the traditional focus in the field. Our
current work provides an entirely new platform for robust desalination under harsh chemical
conditions, expanding the number applications where membrane-based desalination is now
relevant.

ice-water bath (i.e., 273 K) to determine the flux of our MOF-801 membrane whereas a
higher driving force enabled by a liquid nitrogen cold trap (i.e., 77 K) was used in other

membranes is distinctly different from our MOF membranes. Therefore, it makes more sense
to compare the performance of our MOF membrane to other state-of-the-art zeolite and MOF
membranes that belong to an emerging class of polycrystalline molecular sieve membranes

and selectivity of the membranes produced and do not cite “Permeability, permeance and
selectivity: A preferred way of reporting pervaporation performance data” by Richard W.

better reflect intrinsic properties of the membranes. We also added permeance data to the
Supplementary Information (SI) as you see in our response to the next comment.
It should be noted that the reference provided by the reviewer is for pervaporation with
mixtures of organic-organic or organic-water, where the focus is on the selectivity of
separation and permeability-selectivity tradeoff (Journal of Membrane Science 348 (1-2)
(2010) 346-352). However, pervaporation of organic-organic or organic-water is totally
different from pervaporation desalination. Water flux (not permeance) and salt rejection (not
selectivity) are often presented as a metric of comparison in pervaporation desalination
studies (1-14). Due to practical challenges of obtaining accurate data, permeance is not
always reported in open literature as it requires close monitoring of desalination operating
conditions such as trans-membrane pressure difference. In fact, if this information is not
disclosed, permeance can obfuscate the experimental conditions that should be used for a fair
comparison between materials. Therefore, we have adopted the standard practice—which has
been used for other membrane processes like microfiltration and membrane distillation—of
reporting water flux as a simpler parameter directly reflecting water treatment efficiency—
while providing transparency about our experimental conditions and membrane properties
(15-17).
More importantly, the core novel aspects of this work include the precise regulation of
missing linkers, characterization of the atomistic mechanism of enhanced performance, and
harsh chemical operation stability, all of which have not been explored in existing works.

This contribution reports a type of pervaporation membrane, fabricated with MOF-801 thin
